input:
This example considers a vapour-compression unit that serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. A useful starting point is the Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures, which is 6.07 and which represents the upper limit for any cycle operating between 0 °C and 45 °C. The coefficient of performance itself is defined as the refrigeration effect divided by the work input, so the Carnot figure effectively sets the benchmark against which real machines can be judged.

In practice, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.94, corresponding to roughly 48% of the Carnot value of 6.07. The difference between the two figures reflects the various losses that the idealised cycle leaves out, such as pressure drops through the lines and heat exchangers, irreversibility in the compressor, and heat transfer across finite temperature differences in the evaporator and the condenser. It should be emphasised that the manufacturer's figure does not break these contributions down separately, since it is reported as one single test value for the unit as a whole.

Another important consideration is that the manufacturer's test was performed at full load, meaning that the quoted 2.94 applies specifically to that condition. Part-load performance is not stated, which matters because the cold store will not demand full load continuously throughout the year. Under part-load operation, the balance between fixed losses and useful refrigeration changes, and the coefficient of performance changes with it, in a direction that cannot be inferred from the single figure provided. As a result, a seasonal energy estimate that relies on 2.94 will contain an unquantified error, and the value of 2.94 is more appropriately used for comparing units tested under the same conditions than for forecasting running costs. Used in that narrower way, 2.94 remains a meaningful figure; used as a predictor, it promises more than a single full-load test can deliver.
target:
A vapour-compression unit serving a cold store evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C, and its coefficient of performance at full load is 2.94, which is 48% of the Carnot value of 6.07 between the same temperatures. The coefficient of performance is the refrigeration effect divided by the work input. The Carnot value is the highest the ratio can reach for a cycle working between the two temperatures: it is fixed by the temperatures alone, and no machine exceeds it.

The gap between 2.94 and 6.07 is the sum of the losses the ideal cycle omits: pressure drops in the lines and exchangers, irreversibility in the compressor, and heat transfer across finite temperature differences in the evaporator and the condenser. None of these losses is separated in the manufacturer's figure, which is a single test value for the whole unit, and the split between them cannot be recovered from it.

The two temperatures set the limit through the lift the cycle must provide. Heat is taken up at 0 °C and rejected at 45 °C, and every loss inside the machine is paid for across that lift; a wider lift at the same refrigeration duty would lower the Carnot value itself and lower the achieved value with it. The achieved 2.94 is therefore a property of the unit at its stated temperatures, not a rating that transfers to a warmer condenser or a colder evaporator.

The manufacturer's test was run at full load, and the stated 2.94 belongs to that condition. Part-load performance is not stated, and the cold store does not call for full load at all times: at part load the balance between fixed losses and useful refrigeration shifts, and the coefficient of performance moves with it, in a direction the available figure does not fix. A seasonal energy estimate built on 2.94 carries an unquantified error, and the figure supports comparison between units tested the same way rather than a prediction of running cost.
